clinicalPearls: This is the autosomal recessive form of congenital long QT syndrome combining profound bilateral sensorineural deafness with marked QT prolongation and life-threatening ventricular arrhythmia.
It is caused by biallelic variants in KCNQ1 (type 1, most cases) or KCNE1 (type 2), the genes encoding the slow delayed-rectifier potassium channel IKs.

The same potassium current maintains the high-potassium endolymph of the cochlea, so complete loss of channel function abolishes hearing while heterozygous carriers may show only autosomal dominant Romano-Ward long QT without deafness.
Presentation is often in early childhood with syncope, seizures or cardiac arrest triggered by exertion, emotion or fright.
The corrected QT interval is usually very markedly prolonged, considerably longer on average than in Romano-Ward syndrome, conferring a high arrhythmic risk.
Torsades de pointes and ventricular fibrillation are the mechanism of syncope and sudden death; iron-deficiency anaemia and hypokalaemia can worsen risk.
Deafness is congenital, profound and prelingual, and cochlear implantation is frequently required, with careful cardiac monitoring during anaesthesia.
Beta-blockade is the cornerstone of therapy but residual risk is high, so left cardiac sympathetic denervation and implantable defibrillators are often needed.
reference.pathophysiology: Jervell and Lange-Nielsen syndrome is a recessive channelopathy resulting from complete or near-complete loss of the slow delayed-rectifier potassium current IKs, produced when a person inherits two pathogenic alleles of KCNQ1 (the pore-forming alpha subunit, causing type 1) or, less commonly, KCNE1 (the ancillary beta subunit, causing type 2). In cardiac myocytes IKs contributes to phase-3 repolarisation of the action potential; its loss prolongs the action-potential duration and the QT interval, creating a substrate for early after-depolarisations and reentrant torsades de pointes ventricular tachycardia, particularly under adrenergic stress. The identical KCNQ1/KCNE1 channel is expressed in the marginal cells of the stria vascularis, where it secretes potassium into the scala media to generate the potassium-rich endolymph and endocochlear potential essential for hair-cell transduction; biallelic loss collapses this potential, causing endolymphatic degeneration and profound congenital sensorineural deafness. Because heterozygotes retain roughly half the channel function, they typically have normal hearing but may manifest a milder dominant long QT phenotype (Romano-Ward), which explains the recessive inheritance of the combined cardioauditory syndrome and the importance of screening apparently unaffected family members.
additionalDifferentials: Romano-Ward syndrome (autosomal dominant long QT without deafness)
Acquired QT prolongation from drugs or electrolyte disturbance such as hypokalaemia or hypomagnesaemia
Other congenital long QT genotypes including sodium- and potassium-channel subtypes
Catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia presenting with exertional syncope
Pendred syndrome and other causes of congenital sensorineural deafness
Epilepsy misdiagnosed from arrhythmic syncope with convulsive movements
Timothy syndrome and other multisystem arrhythmia syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram with corrected QT measurement and morphology assessment
Exercise and adrenaline provocation testing to unmask QT dynamics
Ambulatory and event ECG monitoring for arrhythmia detection
Genetic testing of KCNQ1 and KCNE1 with cascade screening of relatives
Comprehensive audiological assessment including brainstem-evoked responses
Serum potassium, magnesium and iron studies to correct modifiable arrhythmic risk factors
Echocardiography to exclude structural heart disease
redFlags: Syncope, seizure or aborted cardiac arrest triggered by exercise, emotion or startle
Documented torsades de pointes or ventricular fibrillation
Very markedly prolonged corrected QT interval on electrocardiography
Family history of sudden unexplained death or congenital deafness with cardiac events
Planned anaesthesia or QT-prolonging medication in an unmonitored patient
reference.prognosis: Untreated, the syndrome carries a high risk of sudden cardiac death in childhood; with beta-blockade, avoidance of QT-prolonging drugs and, where indicated, sympathetic denervation and defibrillator implantation, survival improves substantially, although the very long QT of type 1 disease still confers appreciable residual arrhythmic risk.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing arrhythmic syncope as epilepsy and delaying cardiac evaluation
Assessing hearing without an electrocardiogram, so the cardiac component is missed in a deaf child
Administering QT-prolonging drugs or performing anaesthesia without cardiac monitoring
Assuming beta-blockade alone confers full protection despite ongoing high-risk features
Overlooking a milder dominant long QT phenotype in heterozygous relatives who need screening
references: Cardiology guidelines on inherited arrhythmia syndromes
Audiology and paediatric cardiology reference texts
management: Institute long-term non-selective beta-blockade (nadolol or propranolol) as the mainstay to blunt adrenergic-triggered torsades de pointes
Strictly avoid QT-prolonging medications and provide the patient with an up-to-date list of agents to shun
Correct modifiable arrhythmic risk factors by treating hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and iron-deficiency anaemia
Implant a cardioverter-defibrillator in survivors of cardiac arrest or those with breakthrough syncope despite beta-blockade
Consider left cardiac sympathetic denervation for recurrent events on optimal medical therapy
Offer cochlear implantation and audiological rehabilitation for the profound congenital sensorineural deafness
Arrange genetic counselling with cascade ECG and KCNQ1/KCNE1 testing of first-degree relatives
Give a written emergency action plan, restrict competitive and startle-provoking activity, and escalate promptly for syncope or arrhythmia
